prompt: The mean oscillation of a function $f$ on an interval $(a,b)$ is defined to be the average value of $|f(x)-\bar f|$ on $(a,b)$, where $\bar f$ is the average value of $f$ on $(a,b)$. Calculate the mean oscillation of the function $f=\log x$ on the interval $(0,b)$.

solutions.title: Rescale to $(0,1)$
solutions.body:
**Average of $f$.** $\displaystyle\bar f=\frac1b\int_0^b\log x\,dx=\frac1b\big[x\log x-x\big]_0^b=\log b-1$ (the integral is improper but convergent since $x\log x\to0$).

**Mean oscillation.** Substitute $x=bt$, $t\in(0,1)$: $\log x-\bar f=\log b+\log t-\log b+1=\log t+1$. Hence
$$\frac1b\int_0^b|\log x-\bar f|\,dx=\int_0^1|\log t+1|\,dt .$$
The integrand changes sign at $t=1/e$, and $\frac{d}{dt}(t\log t)=\log t+1$, so
$$\int_0^1|\log t+1|\,dt=-\big[t\log t\big]_0^{1/e}+\big[t\log t\big]_{1/e}^{1}=\frac1e+\frac1e=\frac2e .$$
In particular the answer does not depend on $b$ (as expected from scaling: $\log(bx)$ differs from $\log x$ by a constant).

**Answer: $\dfrac{2}{e}\approx0.736$**

solutions.title: Use $\int |h| = 2\int h^+$
solutions.body:
For any integrable $h$ with $\int_0^1 h=0$ we have $\int_0^1|h|=2\int_0^1 h^+$. With $h(t)=\log t+1$ (mean zero on $(0,1)$, by the first solution's computation of $\bar f$ after rescaling), $h>0$ exactly on $(1/e,1)$, so
$$\int_0^1|h|=2\int_{1/e}^1(\log t+1)\,dt=2\big[t\log t\big]_{1/e}^{1}=2\cdot\frac1e=\frac2e .$$
A numerical check with $b=3.7$ gives $0.73576\ldots=2/e$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{2}{e}$**

prompt:
Let $I$ be an open interval, and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be a differentiable function. Assume that $f'(x)\ge0$ for all $x\in I$, and that all zeroes of $f'$ are isolated (this means that if $f'(x_0)=0$ for some $x_0\in I$, then there is some $\epsilon>0$ such that $f'(x)\ne0$ for all $x\in I$ such that $0<|x-x_0|<\epsilon$).

Without using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, show that $f$ is strictly increasing on $I$ (the latter means that $f(x_1)<f(x_2)$ for all $x_1<x_2$ in $I$).

Do not assume that $f'$ is continuous.
answer: By the mean value theorem $f$ is weakly increasing. If $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ with $x_1<x_2$, then $f$ is constant on $[x_1,x_2]$, so $f'=0$ on all of $(x_1,x_2)$, contradicting that zeros of $f'$ are isolated.

solutions.title: Mean value theorem twice
solutions.body:
**Weakly increasing.** Let $x_1<x_2$ in $I$. $f$ is differentiable, hence continuous, on $[x_1,x_2]\subset I$, so by the mean value theorem there is $c\in(x_1,x_2)$ with
$$f(x_2)-f(x_1)=f'(c)(x_2-x_1)\ge0 .$$
So $f(x_1)\le f(x_2)$.

**Strictly increasing.** Suppose $x_1<x_2$ and $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$. For $x\in[x_1,x_2]$, monotonicity gives $f(x_1)\le f(x)\le f(x_2)=f(x_1)$, so $f$ is constant on $[x_1,x_2]$. Hence $f'(x)=0$ for every $x\in(x_1,x_2)$ (the difference quotients at such $x$ are $0$ for small increments). Take $x_0=\frac{x_1+x_2}2$: $f'(x_0)=0$ but every point of $(x_1,x_2)$ near $x_0$ is also a zero of $f'$, so $x_0$ is not an isolated zero. Contradiction.

Therefore $f(x_1)<f(x_2)$ whenever $x_1<x_2$. ∎

(No continuity of $f'$ and no integration were used, only the mean value theorem.)

prompt:
Suppose that $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is a continuous function from the reals to the reals, and let $X\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a subset of the real numbers. For each of the following statements either prove it is always true or give an example to show it can be false.

(a) If $X$ is open then $f(X)$ is open.

(b) If $X$ is closed then $f(X)$ is closed.

(c) If $X$ is open then $f^{-1}(X)$ is open.

(d) If $X$ is closed then $f^{-1}(X)$ is closed.
answer: (a) False: $f(x)=x^2$, $f((-1,1))=[0,1)$. (b) False: $f(x)=\frac1{1+x^2}$, $f(\mathbb R)=(0,1]$. (c) True (from the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ definition). (d) True (take complements in (c)).

solutions.title: Counterexamples and the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ argument
solutions.body:
**(a) False.** $f(x)=x^2$, $X=(-1,1)$ open, but $f(X)=[0,1)$ is not open (no interval around $0$ is contained in it).

**(b) False.** $f(x)=\dfrac1{1+x^2}$, $X=\mathbb R$ closed, but $f(X)=(0,1]$ is not closed ($1/(1+n^2)\to0\notin f(X)$).

**(c) True.** Let $X$ be open and $x_0\in f^{-1}(X)$. Since $f(x_0)\in X$ and $X$ is open, there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $(f(x_0)-\varepsilon,f(x_0)+\varepsilon)\subseteq X$. By continuity at $x_0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $|x-x_0|<\delta$ implies $|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon$, hence $f(x)\in X$. So $(x_0-\delta,x_0+\delta)\subseteq f^{-1}(X)$, and $f^{-1}(X)$ is open.

**(d) True.** If $X$ is closed, $\mathbb R\setminus X$ is open, so by (c) $f^{-1}(\mathbb R\setminus X)=\mathbb R\setminus f^{-1}(X)$ is open; hence $f^{-1}(X)$ is closed. ∎

prompt: How many zeros does the function $4z^{10}+e^z$ have in the open unit disc $\{z:|z|<1\}$ of the complex plane? Prove that it has no multiple zeros.
answer: $10$ zeros (Rouché: $|e^z|\le e<4=|4z^{10}|$ on $|z|=1$). A multiple zero would satisfy $4z^{10}=-e^z=40z^9$, forcing $z=0$ or $z=10$, neither of which is a zero.

solutions.title: Rouché's theorem
solutions.body:
Let $F(z)=4z^{10}+e^z$, $p(z)=4z^{10}$. On $|z|=1$,
$$|e^z|=e^{\mathrm{Re}\,z}\le e<4=|p(z)| .$$
By Rouché's theorem, $F=p+e^z$ and $p$ have the same number of zeros, counted with multiplicity, in $|z|<1$. Since $p$ has a zero of order $10$ at $0$, $F$ has $10$ zeros in the disc counted with multiplicity (and none on $|z|=1$, since there $|F|\ge 4-e>0$).

**No multiple zeros.** A multiple zero satisfies $F(z)=F'(z)=0$, i.e.
$$4z^{10}=-e^z\quad\text{and}\quad 40z^9=-e^z .$$
Then $4z^{10}=40z^9$, i.e. $4z^9(z-10)=0$, so $z=0$ or $z=10$. But $F(0)=1\ne0$ and $F(10)=4\cdot10^{10}+e^{10}>0$. So $F$ has no multiple zeros at all, and its $10$ zeros in the disc are distinct.

**Answer: 10 zeros, all simple.** ∎

(A numerical evaluation of the argument-principle integral $\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z|=1}F'/F\,dz$ indeed gives $10$.)

prompt:
Let $f$ be an analytic function on the real line, and define $g$ by
$$g(s)=\int_0^1 f(t)\,t^s\,dt\qquad\text{for } s>0.$$
Prove that $g$ can be extended to a meromorphic function on the whole complex plane. (Hint: first do the case $f(t)=t^n$.) Where would you expect to find the poles of $g$?
answer: For $f=t^k$, $g(s)=\frac1{s+k+1}$. In general write $f=\sum_{k\le N}a_kt^k+t^{N+1}h_N(t)$ with $h_N$ bounded on $(0,1]$: $g(s)=\sum_{k\le N}\frac{a_k}{s+k+1}+\int_0^1t^{s+N+1}h_N\,dt$, meromorphic for $\mathrm{Re}\,s>-N-2$. Poles can only be simple poles at $s=-1,-2,-3,\dots$; $s=-k-1$ is a pole (residue $f^{(k)}(0)/k!$) iff $f^{(k)}(0)\ne0$.

solutions.title: Peel off Taylor polynomials
solutions.body:
**Monomials.** For $f(t)=t^k$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,s>-k-1$, $\int_0^1t^{s+k}\,dt=\dfrac1{s+k+1}$, which is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$ with a single simple pole at $s=-k-1$.

**A holomorphy lemma.** If $h$ is continuous and bounded on $(0,1]$, $|h|\le M$, and $m\ge0$, then
$$H(s)=\int_0^1t^{s+m}h(t)\,dt$$
is holomorphic on $\{\mathrm{Re}\,s>-m-1\}$. Indeed, on a half-plane $\mathrm{Re}\,s\ge\sigma_0>-m-1$ the integrand is bounded by $M\,t^{\sigma_0+m}$, which is integrable on $(0,1)$; so $H$ is continuous there (dominated convergence), and for any closed triangle $\Delta$ in the half-plane, Fubini and Cauchy's theorem for $s\mapsto t^{s+m}=e^{(s+m)\log t}$ give $\oint_{\partial\Delta}H(s)\,ds=\int_0^1h(t)\oint_{\partial\Delta}t^{s+m}\,ds\,dt=0$. By Morera's theorem $H$ is holomorphic.

**Continuation.** Let $a_k=f^{(k)}(0)/k!$. Since $f$ is analytic (in particular $C^\infty$) on $\mathbb R$, Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder gives, for each $N\ge0$,
$$f(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_kt^k+t^{N+1}h_N(t),\qquad |h_N(t)|\le\frac{\max_{[0,1]}|f^{(N+1)}|}{(N+1)!}\ \ (0<t\le1),$$
with $h_N(t)=\big(f(t)-\sum_{k\le N}a_kt^k\big)/t^{N+1}$ continuous on $(0,1]$. Hence for $s>0$
$$g(s)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}\frac{a_k}{s+k+1}+\int_0^1t^{s+N+1}h_N(t)\,dt=:G_N(s).$$
By the lemma (with $m=N+1$), $G_N$ is meromorphic on $U_N=\{\mathrm{Re}\,s>-N-2\}$, with at most simple poles at $-1,-2,\dots,-N-1$. For $N<N'$, $G_N$ and $G_{N'}$ agree on $(0,\infty)$, hence on the connected set $U_N$ minus the poles, by the identity theorem. So the $G_N$ fit together into one meromorphic function on $\bigcup_NU_N=\mathbb C$ extending $g$.

**Poles.** On $U_N$ the only possible poles are at $s=-k-1$, $0\le k\le N$, coming from $\frac{a_k}{s+k+1}$; the residue there is $a_k$. So $g$ has (at most simple) poles only at $s=-1,-2,-3,\dots$, and $s=-k-1$ is actually a pole exactly when $f^{(k)}(0)\ne0$, with residue $f^{(k)}(0)/k!$. ∎

(Only smoothness of $f$ on $[0,1]$ was used; analyticity is more than enough.)

prompt: Prove that the function taking $A$ to $S=(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}$ is a bijection from orthogonal real matrices $A$ whose eigenvalues are all different from $-1$ to skew-symmetric real matrices $S$.
answer: (Cayley transform.) $S^T=(I+A^{-1})^{-1}(I-A^{-1})=(A+I)^{-1}(A-I)=-S$. Conversely for skew $S$, $I+S$ is invertible ($x^T(I+S)x=|x|^2$) and $A=(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}$ is orthogonal with $I+A=2(I+S)^{-1}$ invertible; the two maps are mutually inverse.

solutions.title: Explicit inverse map
solutions.body:
Throughout, note that $I-A$, $I+A$ and $(I+A)^{-1}$ commute with each other (all are rational functions of $A$); similarly for $S$.

**$S$ is well defined and skew.** $-1$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$, so $I+A$ is invertible. Using $A^T=A^{-1}$,
$$S^T=\big((I+A)^{-1}\big)^T(I-A)^T=(I+A^{-1})^{-1}(I-A^{-1}).$$
Now $I+A^{-1}=A^{-1}(A+I)$ and $I-A^{-1}=A^{-1}(A-I)$, so
$$S^T=(A+I)^{-1}A\cdot A^{-1}(A-I)=(I+A)^{-1}(A-I)=-(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}=-S .$$

**The inverse map.** Let $S$ be real skew-symmetric. For real $x$, $x^TSx=0$ (it equals its own negative), so $x^T(I+S)x=|x|^2>0$ for $x\ne0$; hence $I+S$ is invertible (same for $I-S$). Define $A=(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}$.
- *Orthogonal:* $A^T=(I+S^T)^{-1}(I-S^T)=(I-S)^{-1}(I+S)$, so $A^TA=(I-S)^{-1}(I+S)(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}=I$ (the factors commute).
- *No eigenvalue $-1$:* $I+A=\big((I+S)+(I-S)\big)(I+S)^{-1}=2(I+S)^{-1}$ is invertible.

**Mutually inverse.** Starting from $A$ with $S=(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}$:
$$I+S=2(I+A)^{-1},\qquad I-S=2A(I+A)^{-1},$$
so $(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}=2A(I+A)^{-1}\cdot\tfrac12(I+A)=A$. The same computation with the roles of $A$ and $S$ exchanged (the formulas are symmetric) shows that starting from $S$ and forming $A=(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}$, we get $(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}=S$.

Hence $A\mapsto S$ is a bijection between the two sets, with inverse $S\mapsto(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}$. ∎

prompt: Let $V$ be the vector space of $n$ by $n$ matrices over a field, let $A$ be an element of $V$, and let $T$ be the linear transformation of $V$ taking $X$ to $AX$. Compute the determinant and trace of $T$ in terms of the determinant and trace of $A$.
answer: $\operatorname{tr}T=n\operatorname{tr}A$ and $\det T=(\det A)^n$ ($T$ acts as $A$ on each of the $n$ columns, so its matrix is $A\oplus\cdots\oplus A$).

solutions.title: Act column by column
solutions.body:
Write $X=[x_1|\cdots|x_n]$ in columns. Then $AX=[Ax_1|\cdots|Ax_n]$, so under the isomorphism $V\cong F^n\oplus\cdots\oplus F^n$ ($n$ copies, one per column), $T$ acts as $A$ on each summand. In the basis $E_{11},E_{21},\dots,E_{n1},E_{12},\dots,E_{nn}$ (ordered column by column) the matrix of $T$ is block diagonal:
$$[T]=\begin{pmatrix}A&&\\&\ddots&\\&&A\end{pmatrix}\quad(n\text{ blocks}).$$
Hence
$$\operatorname{tr}T=n\operatorname{tr}A,\qquad \det T=(\det A)^n. \ ∎$$

solutions.title: Matrix units and multiplicativity
solutions.body:
**Trace.** $T(E_{ij})=AE_{ij}=\sum_k a_{ki}E_{kj}$, whose $E_{ij}$-coefficient is $a_{ii}$. Summing over all $i,j$: $\operatorname{tr}T=\sum_{j}\sum_i a_{ii}=n\operatorname{tr}A$.

**Determinant.** Write $L_A(X)=AX$. Since $L_{AB}=L_AL_B$, the map $A\mapsto\det L_A$ is multiplicative. Every matrix is a product of elementary matrices and one diagonal matrix $\mathrm{diag}(d,1,\dots,1)$ (row reduction), so it suffices to check these. For a diagonal $D=\mathrm{diag}(d,1,\dots,1)$, $L_D$ scales the $n$ matrix units $E_{1j}$ by $d$ and fixes the others: $\det L_D=d^n=(\det D)^n$. For an elementary matrix $E=I+cE_{kl}$ ($k\ne l$), $L_E$ is unipotent (it is $I+cL_{E_{kl}}$ with $L_{E_{kl}}^2=L_{E_{kl}^2}=0$), so $\det L_E=1=(\det E)^n$. Hence $\det L_A=(\det A)^n$ for all $A$. ∎

prompt: Prove that any group of order $18$ is a semidirect product of a normal subgroup of order $9$ by a group of order $2$, and use this to classify these groups.
answer: Sylow: $N$ of order $9$ is normal (index 2), and $G=N\rtimes\langle t\rangle$. Actions are involutions in $\mathrm{Aut}(N)$ up to conjugacy: for $N=\mathbb Z_9$, $\pm1$; for $N=\mathbb Z_3^2$, $I$, $\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$, $-I$. Exactly $5$ groups: $\mathbb Z_{18}$, $\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_6$, $D_9$, $\mathbb Z_3\times S_3$, $(\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_3)\rtimes\mathbb Z_2$ (inversion).

solutions.title: Sylow theory and involutions in $\mathrm{Aut}(N)$
solutions.body:
**Semidirect product.** Let $|G|=18=2\cdot3^2$. By Sylow's theorem there is a subgroup $N$ of order $9$; it has index $2$, hence is normal. By Cauchy's theorem there is an element $t$ of order $2$; $H=\langle t\rangle$ satisfies $N\cap H=1$ (orders $9$ and $2$ are coprime) and $|NH|=18$, so $G=NH$. Therefore $G\cong N\rtimes_\theta\mathbb Z_2$ where $\theta(t)=a\in\mathrm{Aut}(N)$, $a(n)=tnt^{-1}$, satisfies $a^2=1$.

A standard fact: if $a'=\psi a\psi^{-1}$ for some $\psi\in\mathrm{Aut}(N)$, then $(n,t^\varepsilon)\mapsto(\psi(n),t^\varepsilon)$ is an isomorphism $N\rtimes_a\mathbb Z_2\to N\rtimes_{a'}\mathbb Z_2$. So we need the conjugacy classes of elements $a$ with $a^2=1$ in $\mathrm{Aut}(N)$. Groups of order $p^2$ are abelian, so $N\cong\mathbb Z_9$ or $\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_3$.

**Case $N=\mathbb Z_9$.** $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb Z_9)\cong(\mathbb Z/9)^\times\cong\mathbb Z_6$ is cyclic, so its only elements with $a^2=1$ are $x\mapsto x$ and $x\mapsto-x$. These give
- $\mathbb Z_9\times\mathbb Z_2\cong\mathbb Z_{18}$,
- the dihedral group $D_9=\langle r,s\mid r^9=s^2=1,\ srs^{-1}=r^{-1}\rangle$.

**Case $N=\mathbb Z_3^2=\mathbb F_3^2$.** $\mathrm{Aut}(N)=GL_2(\mathbb F_3)$. If $a^2=I$ then, since $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ has distinct roots in characteristic $3$, $a$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues $\pm1$; so $a$ is conjugate to exactly one of $I$, $\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$, $-I$ (determined by the dimensions of the two eigenspaces, which sum to $2$). These give
- $\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_2\cong\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_6$,
- $\mathbb Z_3\times(\mathbb Z_3\rtimes\mathbb Z_2)\cong\mathbb Z_3\times S_3$,
- the generalized dihedral group $(\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_3)\rtimes\mathbb Z_2$, with $t$ acting by $n\mapsto n^{-1}$.

**They are pairwise non-isomorphic.** $\mathbb Z_{18}$ and $\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_6$ are the abelian ones, distinguished by having/not having an element of order $9$. Among the non-abelian ones, $N$ is the unique Sylow $3$-subgroup (it is normal), so $G$ has an element of order $9$ iff $N$ is cyclic: this singles out $D_9$. Finally $Z(\mathbb Z_3\times S_3)\supseteq\mathbb Z_3\times1$ is nontrivial, while the generalized dihedral group has trivial center: an element $n\in N$ is central iff $n=tnt^{-1}=n^{-1}$ iff $n=1$, and an element $nt$ is not central because it acts on $N$ by inversion, which is nontrivial.

**Conclusion:** there are exactly **5** groups of order $18$: $\mathbb Z_{18}$, $\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_6$, $D_9$, $\mathbb Z_3\times S_3$, and $(\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_3)\rtimes\mathbb Z_2$. ∎

prompt: Let $G$ be a finite group and $H$ a subgroup not equal to $G$. Prove that there is an element of $G$ not in any conjugate $xHx^{-1}$ of $H$.
answer: There are $[G:N_G(H)]\le[G:H]$ conjugates, all containing $1$, so their union has at most $[G:H](|H|-1)+1=|G|-[G:H]+1<|G|$ elements when $[G:H]\ge2$.

solutions.title: Count the union of the conjugates
solutions.body:
The conjugates of $H$ correspond to cosets of the normalizer $N_G(H)\supseteq H$, so their number is
$$k=[G:N_G(H)]\le[G:H]=:m .$$
Each conjugate has $|H|$ elements, one of which is the identity, shared by all of them. Hence
$$\Big|\bigcup_{x\in G}xHx^{-1}\Big|\le k(|H|-1)+1\le m(|H|-1)+1=|G|-m+1 .$$
Since $H\ne G$, $m\ge2$, so the union has at most $|G|-1<|G|$ elements. Therefore some element of $G$ lies in no conjugate of $H$. ∎

(The finiteness of $G$ is essential: e.g. in $GL_n(\mathbb C)$ every element is conjugate into the proper subgroup of upper triangular matrices.)

prompt:
Find continuous bounded functions $f_n$ on the reals (for $n\ge0$) such that all integrals and sums below are well defined and finite, but
$$\int_{x=0}^{\infty}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}f_n(x)\,dx\ne\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\int_{x=0}^{\infty}f_n(x)\,dx .$$
answer: Take a continuous bump $g\ge0$ supported in $[0,1]$ with $\int g=1$ and $f_n(x)=g(x-n)-g(x-n-1)$: each $\int_0^\infty f_n=0$, but $\sum_nf_n=g$ (telescoping), whose integral is $1$.

solutions.title: Telescoping bumps
solutions.body:
Let $g$ be continuous, vanishing outside $[0,1]$, with $\int_0^1 g=1$; e.g. $g(x)=4\min(x,1-x)$ for $x\in[0,1]$ and $g=0$ elsewhere. Define
$$f_n(x)=g(x-n)-g(x-n-1),\qquad n\ge0 .$$
Each $f_n$ is continuous, bounded, and vanishes outside $[n,n+2]$.

- **Each integral:** $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty f_n=\int_n^{n+1}g(x-n)\,dx-\int_{n+1}^{n+2}g(x-n-1)\,dx=1-1=0$, so $\sum_n\int_0^\infty f_n=0$.
- **The sum:** for fixed $x$, $\sum_{n=0}^{N}f_n(x)=g(x)-g(x-N-1)$, and $g(x-N-1)=0$ as soon as $N+1>x$. So $\sum_{n=0}^\infty f_n(x)=g(x)$ (only finitely many nonzero terms at each $x$), and $\int_0^\infty\sum_nf_n=\int_0^\infty g=1$.

Thus $1\ne0$. (Interchange fails because $\sum_n\int|f_n|=\sum_n2=\infty$, so Fubini/dominated convergence does not apply.) ∎

prompt: Show that it is possible to find an uncountable set of subsets of the positive integers that is totally ordered by inclusion. ("Totally ordered by inclusion" means that given two of these subsets $M,N$ either $M\subseteq N$ or $N\subseteq M$. For example, the subsets $\{1\}\subseteq\{1,2\}\subseteq\{1,2,3\}\subseteq\cdots$ are totally ordered by inclusion, but are only a countable set of subsets.)
answer: Transport Dedekind cuts: fix a bijection $q:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Q$ and let $M_\alpha=\{n:q(n)<\alpha\}$ for $\alpha\in\mathbb R$. Then $\alpha<\beta\Rightarrow M_\alpha\subsetneq M_\beta$, giving an uncountable chain.

solutions.title: Dedekind cuts
solutions.body:
Since $\mathbb Q$ is countably infinite, fix a bijection $q:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Q$. For each real $\alpha$ let
$$M_\alpha=\{n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}: q(n)<\alpha\}.$$
- **Totally ordered:** if $\alpha\le\beta$ then $q(n)<\alpha$ implies $q(n)<\beta$, so $M_\alpha\subseteq M_\beta$. Any two reals are comparable, hence so are any two of the sets.
- **Distinct:** if $\alpha<\beta$, pick a rational $r$ with $\alpha<r<\beta$ (density of $\mathbb Q$); then $q^{-1}(r)\in M_\beta\setminus M_\alpha$. So $\alpha\mapsto M_\alpha$ is injective.

Hence $\{M_\alpha:\alpha\in\mathbb R\}$ is an uncountable family (it is in bijection with $\mathbb R$) of subsets of the positive integers, totally ordered by inclusion. ∎

prompt: Suppose that the functions $g,f_0,f_1,f_2,\dots$ are smooth real valued functions on $\mathbb R$ such that they all vanish at $0$ and $\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n'(x)=g'(x)$ for all $x$. (Here $g'$ means the derivative of $g$.) Either prove or give a counter-example to the claim that $\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n(x)=g(x)$ for all $x$.
answer: False. Let $\phi$ be smooth with $\phi=0$ on $(-\infty,0]$ and $\phi=1$ on $[1,\infty)$, $f_n(x)=\phi(nx)$, $g=0$: $f_n'(x)=n\phi'(nx)=0$ once $n>1/x$ (and for $x\le0$), so $f_n'\to0=g'$ pointwise, but $f_n(x)\to1$ for $x>0$.

solutions.title: A smooth step that steepens
solutions.body:
**The claim is false.**

Let $\psi(x)=e^{-1/x}$ for $x>0$ and $\psi(x)=0$ for $x\le0$; $\psi$ is smooth. Put
$$\phi(x)=\frac{\psi(x)}{\psi(x)+\psi(1-x)},$$
which is smooth (the denominator never vanishes), with $\phi=0$ on $(-\infty,0]$, $\phi=1$ on $[1,\infty)$, so $\phi'=0$ outside $[0,1]$. Let
$$f_n(x)=\phi(nx)\quad(n\ge1),\qquad f_0=0,\qquad g=0 .$$
All are smooth and vanish at $0$.

- **Derivatives converge to $g'=0$ pointwise:** $f_n'(x)=n\phi'(nx)$. If $x\le0$ then $nx\le0$ and $f_n'(x)=0$. If $x>0$ then for $n>1/x$ we have $nx>1$ and $f_n'(x)=0$. So $f_n'(x)\to0=g'(x)$ for every $x$.
- **But the functions do not converge to $g$:** for $x>0$ and $n>1/x$, $f_n(x)=\phi(nx)=1$, so $f_n(x)\to1\ne0=g(x)$.

So pointwise convergence of derivatives (even with a common value at $0$) does not imply convergence of the functions; one needs e.g. uniform convergence of $f_n'$ on intervals. ∎

*Remark.* The official solution uses the step function ($0$ for $x\le0$, $1$ for $x>1/n$), which is not smooth (not even continuous as written); the smoothed version above fixes this.

prompt: Let $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ be an entire function, and suppose that $f(z)/z\to0$ as $|z|\to\infty$. Prove that $f$ is constant.
answer: Cauchy's estimate on $|z|=R$ gives $|f'(a)|\le\sup_{|z-a|=R}|f(z)|/R\to0$; or apply Liouville to the entire function $(f(z)-f(0))/z$, which tends to $0$ at $\infty$.

solutions.title: Cauchy's estimate for $f'$
solutions.body:
Fix $a\in\mathbb C$. By Cauchy's formula on the circle $|z-a|=R$,
$$f'(a)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z-a|=R}\frac{f(z)}{(z-a)^2}\,dz,\qquad\text{so}\qquad |f'(a)|\le\frac{\max_{|z-a|=R}|f(z)|}{R}.$$
Let $\varepsilon>0$. By hypothesis there is $R_\varepsilon$ with $|f(z)|\le\varepsilon|z|$ for $|z|\ge R_\varepsilon$. For $R\ge R_\varepsilon+|a|$, every $z$ with $|z-a|=R$ has $|z|\ge R_\varepsilon$ and $|z|\le R+|a|$, so
$$|f'(a)|\le\frac{\varepsilon(R+|a|)}{R}\xrightarrow[R\to\infty]{}\varepsilon .$$
Hence $|f'(a)|\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, i.e. $f'(a)=0$. As $a$ was arbitrary, $f'\equiv0$ and $f$ is constant. ∎

solutions.title: Liouville's theorem
solutions.body: Let $h(z)=\dfrac{f(z)-f(0)}{z}$ for $z\ne0$ and $h(0)=f'(0)$. Then $h$ is entire (removable singularity at $0$). As $|z|\to\infty$, $h(z)=\frac{f(z)}{z}-\frac{f(0)}{z}\to0$. So $h$ is bounded outside some disc, and continuous on the disc, hence bounded on $\mathbb C$; by Liouville, $h$ is constant, and the constant is $\lim_{z\to\infty}h=0$. Thus $f(z)=f(0)$ for all $z$. ∎

prompt:
Let $a>0$ be a constant $\ne3$. Let $C_a$ denote the positively oriented circle of radius $a$ centered on the origin. Evaluate
$$\int_{C_a}\frac{z^3+\sin z}{z^3(z-3)}\,dz .$$
(Your answer should be a function of $a$.)
answer: $-\dfrac{2\pi i}{9}$ for $0<a<3$, and $\dfrac{2\pi i\,(24+\sin3)}{27}$ for $a>3$ (residues $-\tfrac19$ at $0$ and $1+\tfrac{\sin3}{27}$ at $3$).

solutions.title: Residues at $0$ and $3$
solutions.body:
Let $g(z)=\dfrac{z^3+\sin z}{z^3(z-3)}=\dfrac1{z-3}+\dfrac{\sin z}{z^3(z-3)}$. It is holomorphic except at $z=0$ and $z=3$.

**At $z=3$:** a simple pole with residue $\dfrac{3^3+\sin3}{3^3}=1+\dfrac{\sin3}{27}$.

**At $z=0$:** $\frac1{z-3}$ is holomorphic there. For the second term,
$$\frac{\sin z}{z^3}=\frac1{z^2}-\frac16+O(z^2),\qquad \frac1{z-3}=-\frac13\cdot\frac{1}{1-z/3}=-\frac13\Big(1+\frac z3+\frac{z^2}9+\cdots\Big).$$
The coefficient of $z^{-1}$ in the product comes only from $\frac1{z^2}\cdot\big(-\frac13\cdot\frac z3\big)$, so
$$\operatorname{Res}_{z=0}g=-\frac19 .$$

**Residue theorem.**
- $0<a<3$: only $z=0$ is inside, so the integral is $2\pi i\cdot\big(-\frac19\big)=-\dfrac{2\pi i}{9}$.
- $a>3$: both poles are inside: $2\pi i\Big(-\dfrac19+1+\dfrac{\sin3}{27}\Big)=\dfrac{2\pi i\,(24+\sin3)}{27}$.

**Answer:** $-\dfrac{2\pi i}{9}$ if $0<a<3$; $\ \dfrac{2\pi i(24+\sin 3)}{27}$ if $a>3$.

solutions.title: Partial fractions check
solutions.body:
Partial fractions give
$$\frac1{z^3(z-3)}=-\frac1{3z^3}-\frac1{9z^2}-\frac1{27z}+\frac1{27(z-3)} .$$
Multiplying by $\sin z=z-\frac{z^3}6+\cdots$, the $z^{-1}$ coefficient at $0$ comes only from $-\frac1{9z^2}\cdot z$ (the terms $-\frac{\sin z}{3z^3}$ and $-\frac{\sin z}{27z}$ contain only even powers of $z$, and the last term is holomorphic at $0$): residue $-\frac19$, as before. The residue at $3$ is $\frac{\sin3}{27}$ from this part plus $1$ from $\frac1{z-3}$.

A direct numerical evaluation of the contour integral gives $-0.69813\,i=-2\pi i/9$ for $a=1$ and $5.61789\,i=2\pi i(24+\sin3)/27$ for $a=5$.

reviewNote: The official solution gives 2πi/9 (a<3) and 2πi(30+sin 3)/27 (a>3), but its expansion uses 1/(1-z/3) = 1 - z/3 + ..., a sign error; the residue at 0 is -1/9 (confirmed by partial fractions and numerical integration), so the corrected values -2πi/9 and 2πi(24+sin 3)/27 are used.

prompt: Let $A$ be the $n$ by $n$ complex matrix whose diagonal entries are all $a$ and whose non-diagonal entries are all $b$. Find the eigenvalues of $A$ and their multiplicities.
answer: $a+(n-1)b$ with multiplicity $1$ (eigenvector $(1,\dots,1)$) and $a-b$ with multiplicity $n-1$ (eigenspace $x_1+\dots+x_n=0$); if $b=0$ these merge into $a$ with multiplicity $n$.

solutions.title: Write $A=(a-b)I+bJ$
solutions.body:
Let $J$ be the all-ones matrix, so $A=(a-b)I+bJ$. $J$ has rank $1$: $J\mathbf 1=n\mathbf 1$ for $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)^T$, and $Jx=0$ for every $x$ in the $(n-1)$-dimensional subspace $W=\{x:\ x_1+\cdots+x_n=0\}$. Since $\mathbb C^n=\mathbb C\mathbf 1\oplus W$, $J$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues $n$ (multiplicity $1$) and $0$ (multiplicity $n-1$).

Adding $(a-b)I$ shifts every eigenvalue by $a-b$ with the same eigenvectors:
- $A\mathbf 1=\big(a+(n-1)b\big)\mathbf 1$: eigenvalue $a+(n-1)b$, multiplicity $1$;
- $Ax=(a-b)x$ for $x\in W$: eigenvalue $a-b$, multiplicity $n-1$.

(Algebraic and geometric multiplicities agree since $A$ is diagonalizable. If $b=0$ the two values coincide and $A=aI$ has the single eigenvalue $a$ with multiplicity $n$.) ∎

solutions.title: Characteristic polynomial
solutions.body:
$\det(A-\lambda I)$: add all rows to the first row; every entry of the first row becomes $a+(n-1)b-\lambda$. Factor this out, then subtract $b$ times the new first row (all ones) from each other row, leaving an upper triangular matrix with diagonal $1,a-b-\lambda,\dots,a-b-\lambda$. Hence
$$\det(A-\lambda I)=\big(a+(n-1)b-\lambda\big)(a-b-\lambda)^{n-1},$$
confirming the eigenvalues $a+(n-1)b$ (multiplicity $1$) and $a-b$ (multiplicity $n-1$). ∎

prompt: Prove that if $A$ is a real $n$ by $n$ matrix then the series $\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}A^m/m!$ converges. (This means for each $i,j$, the sum of $(i,j)$th entries converges.)
answer: With the operator norm, $\|A^m\|\le\|A\|^m$ and $|(A^m)_{ij}|\le\|A^m\|$, so each entry series is dominated by $\sum\|A\|^m/m!=e^{\|A\|}$ and converges absolutely.

solutions.title: Compare with the scalar exponential
solutions.body:
Use the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^n$ and the operator norm $\|M\|=\sup_{|v|=1}|Mv|$ on matrices. It is submultiplicative, $\|MN\|\le\|M\|\,\|N\|$, so $\|A^m\|\le\|A\|^m$. Each entry is bounded by the norm: $|M_{ij}|=|e_i\cdot Me_j|\le|Me_j|\le\|M\|$.

Hence for each fixed $i,j$,
$$\sum_{m=0}^\infty\left|\frac{(A^m)_{ij}}{m!}\right|\le\sum_{m=0}^\infty\frac{\|A\|^m}{m!}=e^{\|A\|}<\infty,$$
so the series of $(i,j)$ entries converges absolutely, hence converges. ∎

solutions.title: Elementary entry bound
solutions.body: Let $c=\max_{i,j}|a_{ij}|$. By induction, every entry of $A^m$ has absolute value at most $n^{m-1}c^m\le (nc)^m$ for $m\ge1$: indeed $|(A^{m+1})_{ij}|=\big|\sum_k(A^m)_{ik}a_{kj}\big|\le n\cdot n^{m-1}c^m\cdot c$. So the $(i,j)$ entry series is dominated by $\sum_m(nc)^m/m!=e^{nc}$ and converges absolutely. ∎

answer: If $r=\sqrt3+\sqrt[3]2\in\mathbb Q$, then $(r-\sqrt3)^3=2$ gives $\sqrt3=\dfrac{r^3+9r-2}{3r^2+3}\in\mathbb Q$, a contradiction. (Or: $\sqrt3\in\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$ is impossible since $2\nmid3$.)

solutions.title: Field degrees (official approach)
solutions.body:
$x^2-3$ and $x^3-2$ are irreducible over $\mathbb Q$ (Eisenstein at $3$ and at $2$), so $[\mathbb Q(\sqrt3):\mathbb Q]=2$ and $[\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2):\mathbb Q]=3$.

Suppose $r=\sqrt3+\sqrt[3]2\in\mathbb Q$. Then $\sqrt3=r-\sqrt[3]2\in\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$, so $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)\subseteq\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$ and by the tower law $2=[\mathbb Q(\sqrt3):\mathbb Q]$ divides $3=[\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2):\mathbb Q]$. Contradiction. ∎

solutions.title: Cube and isolate $\sqrt3$
solutions.body:
Suppose $r=\sqrt3+\sqrt[3]2$ is rational. Then $\sqrt[3]2=r-\sqrt3$, and cubing,
$$2=r^3-3\sqrt3\,r^2+9r-3\sqrt3=(r^3+9r)-\sqrt3\,(3r^2+3).$$
Since $3r^2+3>0$,
$$\sqrt3=\frac{r^3+9r-2}{3r^2+3}\in\mathbb Q,$$
contradicting the irrationality of $\sqrt3$ (if $\sqrt3=p/q$ in lowest terms then $p^2=3q^2$ forces $3\mid p$, then $3\mid q$). ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, written additively. Assume that for each positive integer $n$ the set $\{a\in G: na=0\}$ has at most $n$ elements.

(a) Prove that $G$ is cyclic.

(b) Deduce from this that the multiplicative group of every finite field is cyclic.
answer: (a) If $G\cong\mathbb Z_{n_1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb Z_{n_s}$ with $1<n_1\mid\cdots\mid n_s$ and $s\ge2$, then $n_1a=0$ has $n_1^s>n_1$ solutions. (Or: an element of maximal order $m$ has $mG=0$, so $|G|\le m$.) (b) In a field $x^n=1$ has at most $n$ roots, so $F^\times$ satisfies (a).

solutions.title: Structure theorem (official approach)
solutions.body:
**(a)** Suppose $G$ is not cyclic (in particular $G\ne0$). By the structure theorem for finite abelian groups, $G\cong\mathbb Z/n_1\times\cdots\times\mathbb Z/n_s$ with $1<n_1\mid n_2\mid\cdots\mid n_s$, and $s\ge2$ because $G$ is not cyclic. In each factor $\mathbb Z/n_i$ (where $n_1\mid n_i$) the equation $n_1x=0$ has exactly $n_1$ solutions, so $\{a\in G: n_1a=0\}$ has $n_1^s>n_1$ elements, violating the hypothesis with $n=n_1$. Hence $G$ is cyclic.

**(b)** Let $F$ be a finite field and $G=F^\times$ (written multiplicatively). For each $n\ge1$, the elements with $a^n=1$ are roots of $x^n-1$, a nonzero polynomial of degree $n$ over a field, so there are at most $n$ of them. By (a), $F^\times$ is cyclic. ∎

solutions.title: Element of maximal order
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $g\in G$ have maximal order $m$.

*Lemma.* In a finite abelian group, the order of every element divides the maximal order $m$. Proof: suppose $h$ has order $k\nmid m$. Then some prime $p$ has $p^\beta\,\|\,k$, $p^\alpha\,\|\,m$ with $\beta>\alpha$. The element $p^\alpha g$ has order $m/p^\alpha$ (coprime to $p$) and $(k/p^\beta)h$ has order $p^\beta$; in an abelian group, elements of coprime orders $u,v$ have a sum of order $uv$. So $G$ has an element of order $p^\beta m/p^\alpha>m$, a contradiction.

Hence $ma=0$ for all $a\in G$, so $\{a: ma=0\}=G$ and the hypothesis gives $|G|\le m$. But $\langle g\rangle$ already has $m$ elements, so $G=\langle g\rangle$ is cyclic.

**(b)** As in the first solution: $x^n-1$ has at most $n$ roots in a field. ∎
